questions.q: Northbridge needs to filter the carrier's shipment list by order ID without changing any data. Which request type and mechanism are correct?
options: POST with the order ID in a JSON body
GET with the order ID passed via the params argument
GET with the order ID hardcoded into the function name
POST with the order ID in the URL path only
questions.explain: Reading data without changing anything is a GET request, and filters belong in query parameters, which requests builds for you from the params dictionary.

questions.q: What does passing json=payload to requests.post() do that passing data=payload does not?
options: It sends the request as plain text instead of JSON
It serializes the dictionary to JSON and sets the Content-Type header automatically
It skips sending the request body entirely
It converts the request into a GET request
questions.explain: The json= argument serializes the Python dictionary into a JSON string and sets Content-Type: application/json for you, which data= does not do on its own.

questions.q: Why call response.raise_for_status() instead of only checking response.json()?
options: raise_for_status() is required before .json() will work at all
It makes the request run faster
It raises an exception on a 4xx or 5xx response, catching failures before you trust the body as valid data
It automatically retries failed requests
questions.explain: raise_for_status() turns an error response into a Python exception immediately, so you don't accidentally parse an error page or empty body as if it were valid JSON.

questions.q: The carrier's shipment list caps each response at 100 results and includes a next field. What's the correct way to collect every shipment?
options: Increase the timeout until the server returns everything in one call
Call the endpoint once and assume 100 results is the full list
Loop: request the current page, extend your results, and follow next until it's None
Send the same GET request 100 times in a row
questions.explain: Pagination requires following the next link across repeated requests until the API signals there are no more pages, typically by returning None or omitting the field.

questions.q: What does response.json() return in Python?
options: A raw bytes object
A plain string containing the response text
A Python dictionary (or list) parsed from the response's JSON body
The HTTP status code as an integer
questions.explain: response.json() parses the response body as JSON and returns the equivalent Python data structure, usually a dict, so you can access fields like normal dictionary keys.
